enrichment.short_title: Personal loan recovery against debtor who acknowledged debts but raised ultra vires and limitation defences
key_facts: Mr Mahtani claimed about US$637,298 under a January 1995 agreement and US$265,000 under a separate arrangement relating to shares purchased for Keith Billington.
Billington received the money and repeatedly promised repayment; the corporate claimant Sterling Bureau de Change was joined only by way of caution.
The defendant argued the lender was the company not Mr Mahtani personally, that a company loan would be illegal under Zambian law, and that the second claim was time-barred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Queen's Bench Division on disputed contractual and limitation issues after long-running debt.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Mr Mahtani on principal and compound interest; limitation defence rejected on the basis of part payments; no effective written acknowledgment under ss 29 and 30.
enrichment.ratio: Where contemporaneous documents and conduct show the debt was owed personally to Mr Mahtani, a signature 'for and on behalf of Sterling Bureau Limited' does not displace that objective construction; limitation is not a bar where part payments were made and no qualifying signed written acknowledgment was established.

Whether a loan by the bureau would have been unlawful under Zambian law
Whether interest was simple or compound
Whether a second agreement existed for the US$265,000 share purchase debt
Whether the second agreement was barred by limitation

enrichment.short_title: Farm business tenancy permitted milking and dairying despite 'permanent pasture for livestock only' clause
key_facts: The Bryants sold Meadlands Farm to the Fields subject to a farm business tenancy allowing the Bryants to remain on the land until June 1999 and in buildings until July 1997.
Clause 4.1(a) restricted use to agricultural purposes and clause 4.1(b) required use for permanent pasture for livestock only.
The county court held the FBT did not permit a milking and dairying enterprise; the Bryants' counterclaim for breach of clause 5.6 was dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from preliminary issue declarations at trial in Taunton County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations discharged; counterclaim reinstated; declaration that the FBT permits milking and dairying on the farm land.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 4.1(b) regulates how land is farmed (permanent pasture) rather than prohibiting ancillary dairy use; read against the background that the Bryants had run a dairy herd on the holding and were to retain the land for two years, it did not exclude continued milking and dairying using the relocated sheep house.
legal_issues: Whether 'livestock' in clause 4.1(b) included a dairy herd
Whether clause 4.1(b) prohibited milking after vacation of the farmhouse and buildings
Whether clause 5.6's silence on dairy use in the relocated sheep house was decisive
How clauses 4.1(a) and (b) interact on construction

enrichment.short_title: Murder appeal dismissed where diminished responsibility defence was available but not run at trial
key_facts: Peter Sharp was convicted of murdering Joy Taylor and attempting to murder Leslie Taylor in November 1991 after a breakdown of his relationship with Mrs Taylor.
At trial he ran an accident defence rather than diminished responsibility despite long-term Halcion use and psychiatric evidence.
The CCRC referred the case on whether diminished responsibility should now be considered; fresh psychiatric evidence was adduced on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on a reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission against a 1992 Maidstone Crown Court murder conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; fresh evidence of diminished responsibility not admitted; conviction held safe.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant who chooses not to run diminished responsibility at trial cannot ordinarily raise a different defence on appeal many years later unless exceptional circumstances apply: here Sharp deliberately pursued accident, psychiatric evidence was available before trial, and disputed fresh evidence does not meet the stringent tests in Campbell, Ahluwalia, Straw, Borthwick and Weekes.
legal_issues: Whether fresh psychiatric evidence established diminished responsibility
Why diminished responsibility was not run at trial
Whether the court should receive new medical evidence on appeal
How Campbell and related authorities limit changing defence on appeal

enrichment.short_title: Extradition arrest did not justify common law search of girlfriend's flat two hours later
key_facts: Hewitson was arrested near Jane Passierb's Poole flat on a Bow Street extradition warrant following French cannabis smuggling allegations.
About two hours later police searched the flat under PACE s 32, seizing items including a letter from co-accused Andrew Wright.
The claimant challenged the seizure; the police accepted common law powers as stated in Rottman did not cover these facts but argued for extension of the common law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review hearing in the Administrative Court before Mr Justice Jackson, with Lord Justice Rose agreeing.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; search and seizure unlawful; mandatory order for return of seven listed items and £100 damages.
enrichment.ratio: For extradition arrests PACE search powers do not apply and only surviving common law powers from Ghani v Jones and Rottman remain; those powers do not extend to searching a third party's flat after arrest at a distance, following delay, where the link to the premises is tenuous—the court should not incrementally expand common law search powers to cover such circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether PACE s 32 authorised the search
Whether common law search powers applied to extradition arrests
Whether arrest away from the curtilage of the premises limited search power
Whether delay and tenuous occupancy link defeated legality
Whether the court should develop the common law further

enrichment.short_title: North Bersted housing allocation quashed for failure to hold modifications inquiry and review infrastructure

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Bersted Parish Council challenged SITE6 of the Arun District Local Plan 2003 allocating North Bersted for housing increased from 350 to 650 dwellings.
After a long local plan inquiry the inspector recommended at least 300 additional dwellings subject to infrastructure review; the council adopted 650 without that precondition being satisfied.
The council deferred and then failed properly to consider whether a second inquiry into proposed modifications was required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 287 of the 1990 Act to quash part of an adopted local plan.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; order quashing the North Bersted housing allocation; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority must properly consider whether to hold a further inquiry into objections to proposed modifications before adopting them; here that decision was never lawfully addressed and the council misread the inspector's conditional recommendation on infrastructure as deferrable to a development brief, so adoption of the increased allocation was outside powers.

Whether the inspector's infrastructure review was a precondition to increasing the allocation
Whether misinterpretation of the inspector's report rendered adoption unlawful
Exercise of discretion to grant quashing relief under section 287

enrichment.short_title: Identity-theft convictions for obtaining banking services by deception upheld on payment understanding
key_facts: Sofroniou operated bank accounts and credit cards using false identities of Andrew Cole, John Groves and Andrew Narramore.
He was convicted on nine of ten counts including obtaining services by deception under section 1 of the 1978 Act.
The appeal on counts 1, 2, 4 and 5 challenged whether banking use constituted 'services' and whether there was an understanding that payment would be made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction on counts 1 to 5 with leave; count 3 appeal abandoned.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions on counts 1, 2, 4 and 5 held safe.
enrichment.ratio: Dishonestly operating a bank account or using a credit card over a period can constitute obtaining services under section 1 where there is a putative objective mutual understanding that identifiable payment will be made; inferred overdraft interest or credit charges may suffice, but gratuitous use without such understanding does not—following Shortland and the clarification effected by section 1(3).
legal_issues: Whether opening or operating bank accounts amounts to obtaining services
Whether continuing dishonest use is a continuing offence or duplicitous
What 'understanding that the benefit has been or will be paid for' requires
Relationship between section 1 of the 1978 Act and Halai, Preddy and related theft provisions

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient four-month contempt sentences increased to eight months for repeated injunction breaches
key_facts: The husband repeatedly breached non-molestation orders under section 42 protecting his wife from domestic violence.
Parallel criminal proceedings under the Protection from Harassment Act ran alongside committal applications; overlapping incidents sometimes attracted both processes.
Judge Harris sentenced four months concurrent for two admitted breaches; the wife appealed to increase sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Automatic appeal to the Court of Appeal against sentences for contempt of court in Liverpool County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Sentences increased from four months to eight months concurrent on each admitted breach; guidance given on managing parallel family and criminal proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: The court may increase an unduly lenient committal sentence for breach of a section 42 injunction, applying principles akin to Attorney-General references with double jeopardy adjustment; parallel Protection from Harassment Act proceedings must be coordinated so a defendant is not punished twice for the same act, with the first-sentencing court not discounting for anticipated later sentences.
legal_issues: Whether the court could increase contempt sentences on the wife's appeal
Interaction between Family Law Act injunction committals and Protection from Harassment Act prosecutions
How sentencing ranges compare between family contempt and criminal harassment offences
Avoiding double punishment for the same conduct

enrichment.short_title: Murder and perverting justice convictions safe after Southgate College gang stabbing trial
key_facts: Violence near Southgate College on 13 September 1999 led to Abdul Osman being fatally stabbed and others wounded in a clash between Somalian and Asian student groups.
Bodrul Miah was convicted of murder; Avinash Aubeelack of attempted wounding with intent; Basharath Miah of procuring Bodrul's flight to Bangladesh two days later.
Appeals challenged provocation and lies directions (Bodrul), identification/no case to answer (Aubeelack), and refusal to sever father and son trials (Basharath).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for leave to appeal against conviction following refusal by the single judge; substantive appeals heard by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: All three appeals dismissed; convictions held safe.
enrichment.ratio: Provocation directions may refer to CS gas, blows and stabbing without repeating every fact where the jury has already been directed on self-defence; Smith (Morgan) permits flexible jury directions on characteristics; Richens/Lucas directions on lies must distinguish homicide from provocation issues but need not be elaborate where lies plainly relate only to denial of stabbing; severance under section 5(3) was rightly refused where charges shared the same factual foundation.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately linked provocation directions to the facts including Bodrul being stabbed
Whether characteristics age, sex and height were wrongly excluded under Smith (Morgan)
Whether Lucas/Richens directions on lies and provocation were deficient
Whether Aubeelack had no case to answer on attempted wounding identification
Whether Basharath's trial should have been severed from Bodrul's

enrichment.short_title: Monaco Ferrari auction misstatement claim must be pursued in Monaco under PIL 1995
key_facts: Mr Morin, an English-resident antiques dealer, bought a 1959 Ferrari at a Bonhams auction in Monaco relying on catalogue mileage of 16,626 km.
The vendor later said mileage referred to the period after a 1969 engine overhaul; the car suffered serious engine wear.
Morin sought to sue the Monégasque auctioneer BBM and English parent BBL in England; catalogue conditions chose Monegasque law and non-exclusive Monegasque jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Commercial Court decision on service out of the jurisdiction and setting aside service on BBL.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to serve BBM out of the jurisdiction refused; service on BBL set aside; appropriate forum Monaco.
enrichment.ratio: For negligent misstatement where reliance and loss continued through successful bidding in Monaco, the most significant elements of the tort occurred in Monaco so section 11(2)(c) of the 1995 Act points to Monegasque law; England is not the appropriate forum and a properly arguable joint tortfeasor claim against BBL does not alter that conclusion.
legal_issues: Which country's law governed the tort under sections 11 and 12 of the 1995 Act
Where the most significant elements of negligent misstatement occurred
Whether BBL was a joint tortfeasor with BBM
Whether England was the appropriate forum for trial
Effect of auction conditions excluding warranties and choosing Monegasque law

enrichment.short_title: Care and freeing orders made after judge wrongly adjourned by prioritising adoption over care
key_facts: Baby S, born June 2002, was accommodated from 17 days old with foster carers Mr and Mrs A after his parents could not care for him due to mental illness.
The local authority planned adoption; late in proceedings paternal cousins Mr and Mrs C offered to care for S within the wider family.
The judge adjourned for assessment of the cousins but approached the decision by asking whether the father unreasonably withheld adoption consent rather than first deciding the care application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal by the child's guardian with permission of Hale LJ against adjournment of care and freeing proceedings in Coventry County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; care order made; father’s consent dispensed with; S freed for adoption.
enrichment.ratio: Care and freeing applications must be decided sequentially: the court first determines threshold and where the child should live on welfare grounds; only if a care order is made may it consider dispensing with consent to adoption—allowing the adoption question to dominate an adjournment application is a reversible error of principle.
legal_issues: Correct sequence for care order and freeing for adoption applications
Whether adjournment for kinship assessment was justified
Whether breaking S's attachment to foster carers was outweighed by family placement
Whether the father's withholding of consent to adoption was unreasonable
